screens.title: Introduction to Solidity and the EVM
screens.narratorSegment: Welcome. In this chapter we explore Solidity, the contract-oriented language used to write transparent, immutable logic on Ethereum-compatible blockchains, and the Ethereum Virtual Machine that executes compiled contracts. You will learn how high-level Solidity maps to EVM bytecode, why the pragma directive locks a compiler range, and how gas measures the computational cost of every operation. Understanding these ideas helps you design secure, efficient contracts that deploy and run predictably. For example, a simple storage contract shows how state variables are written to the blockchain and how view functions can be used to read state without gas under a read-only call. A critical contrast to keep in mind is immutability: deployed contracts cannot be edited, so bugs must be prevented ahead of time. Finally, gas is both a fee and a safety: it compensates validators and prevents runaway code. As you go through this lesson set, you will compile a small counter contract, observe gas implications, and practice spotting common mistakes. By the end, you should be able to describe Solidity’s role, explain the EVM’s execution model, and reason about gas and cost trade-offs when designing contracts. What part of building a contract feels most uncertain to you right now?

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Practice and Safety
screens.narratorSegment: This second objectives screen focuses on practice and safety. You will compile example contracts using a compiler version that matches the pragma directive, and you will run read-only calls to view functions without spending gas via a read provider. Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › Practice & Safety

Learning Objectives — Practice and Safety

Practice Steps
  1. Match the compiler version to the pragma and compile the sample contract until there are no warnings.
  2. Run a read-only call to a view function to observe that no gas is consumed by the caller when using a read provider.
  3. Deploy the counter contract and call increment to observe gas usage for state changes.
  4. Test edge cases such as decrement at zero to see safe guards in practice.
Safety Notes
  • Treat deployed contracts as immutable — plan upgrades or use proxy patterns later.
  • Do not store secrets in state variables; anyone can read on-chain data.
  • Think about gas costs when designing frequently executed paths.

screens.title: What is Solidity?
screens.narratorSegment: Solidity is a high-level, contract-oriented language specifically designed to declare the rules, storage, and callable behavior of smart contracts on Ethereum and compatible chains. It borrows familiar syntax patterns from languages like JavaScript and C++ while adding contract-focused keywords and constructs. Define contracts like classes: they bundle state variables, functions, events, and access modifiers into a single deployable unit. A clear definition helps: Solidity is statically typed, which means every variable has a declared type such as an unsigned integer of 256 bits, and the compiler checks types before producing bytecode. For a concrete example, declaring a public uint256 variable creates both storage on-chain and an automatically generated getter function; that getter can be used off-chain without paying gas when called as a read. A common misconception is that Solidity behaves exactly like general-purpose scripting languages — it does not. Contracts run in a distributed, deterministic environment where every state change is recorded and costs gas. Another important point is that code compiled with one compiler version may behave differently under another, so the pragma directive matters for reproducible compilation. As you learn Solidity, practice by reading small contracts and mapping each keyword to its runtime consequence. What part of Solidity’s types or contract model do you want to inspect next?

keyIdea.text: A purpose-built, statically typed language for writing on-chain contracts that compile to EVM bytecode.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › What is Solidity?

What is Solidity?

A contract-oriented, statically typed language tailored for immutable on-chain logic.

Definition & Features
  • Contract-oriented: contracts group state and behavior into deployable units.
  • Statically typed: variable types are declared and checked at compile time.
  • Influenced by C++, Python, and JavaScript syntax, but with blockchain-specific keywords.
  • Compiled to EVM bytecode for deterministic execution across nodes.
Concrete example
Declaring uint256 public myNumber creates storage and an auto-generated getter accessible from off-chain readers without spending gas when called as a read-only operation.
Key Takeaway

Solidity maps high-level declarations to on-chain state and executable bytecode; types and visibility affect storage and access.

Analogy & Misconception

Think of a contract as a vending machine with defined buttons and a transparent inventory. The vending machine’s code can’t be altered after deployment without a planned upgrade. A common misconception is to treat Solidity like ephemeral script: instead, its state and behavior persist on-chain and require careful type and access control design.

Check your understanding
Why is static typing helpful for contracts?
Name one thing that becomes public when you mark a state variable public.

screens.title: Ethereum Virtual Machine (EVM)
screens.narratorSegment: The Ethereum Virtual Machine, or EVM, is the runtime that executes compiled smart contract bytecode on every full node. It behaves like a sandboxed, stack-based virtual machine: contracts are compiled from Solidity into low-level instructions that the EVM understands, and every node runs the same instructions deterministically. This deterministic behavior is essential so that all nodes reach the same state after processing identical transactions. The EVM also isolates contract execution from the host environment, preventing arbitrary node-level access. A concrete example: when you call a function that updates a state variable, the compiled bytecode executes a sequence of stack operations and storage writes; those writes are recorded as state changes only if the transaction completes within the provided gas budget. A common misconception is that the EVM is a centralized server — it is not; it is a runtime implemented by many independent nodes that apply the same rules. Why does this matter in practice? Determinism allows you to reason about contract outcomes and design tests that replicate on-chain behavior. One practical takeaway is to keep bytecode size and complexity reasonable, because more complex operations mean more gas and larger attack surface. After studying the EVM’s role, consider how your high-level code translates to low-level steps and how that affects cost and security.

keyIdea.title: EVM role
keyIdea.text: A deterministic, sandboxed runtime that executes bytecode consistently on every node and enforces resource usage via gas.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › Ethereum Virtual Machine

Ethereum Virtual Machine (EVM)

A sandboxed, deterministic stack machine that runs compiled bytecode on every node.

Architecture Overview
The EVM executes instructions that manipulate a stack, memory, and persistent storage. Every node applies the same rules so that given identical inputs the resulting state is identical across the network.
  • Stack-based execution: operations push and pop values on a stack.
  • Memory vs. storage: memory is ephemeral during execution; storage persists on-chain.
  • Gas enforces limits and compensates validators for work.
Practical note
Because the EVM executes low-level bytecode, high-level constructs that look simple can generate many instructions and cost gas. Keep critical paths efficient.
Concrete Walkthrough
Imagine calling a setter function that updates a state variable. The compiler turns the function into bytecode that reads the input, writes to storage slots, and emits any events. Each low-level step consumes gas, and if the transaction exhausts its gas limit before completion, the EVM reverts state changes while miners keep the gas payment up to that point.
Misconception
The EVM is not a single server. It is a specification implemented by many nodes so determinism and consensus matter for correctness.

screens.title: Compilation: Solidity to Bytecode
screens.narratorSegment: Compilation transforms Solidity source into deployable bytecode that the EVM executes. The process begins with parsing your source file and checking types and syntax against the declared pragma range. The compiler then performs optimization and emits EVM bytecode plus optional metadata. Practically, you compile a file, inspect compiler output for warnings, and produce an artifact that can be deployed. A concrete example: writing a setter function in Solidity compiles down to a sequence of storage write opcodes in bytecode. One common misconception is that compilation is lossless in terms of developer intent; while semantics remain, optimizations can combine or reorder operations to reduce gas. That is why matching the compiler version specified by pragma is crucial — different versions may optimize differently or change semantics. In the Remix IDE you choose a compiler version that satisfies the pragma and view compilation warnings. A useful practice is to read the compiled bytecode size and the ABI. The ABI tells external callers how to encode function calls; the bytecode is what the EVM runs. As a closing thought, compiling is where abstraction meets execution, so use compilation as a safety gate: ensure warnings are addressed and the pragma is aligned with your selected compiler.

keyIdea.text: Solidity source is type-checked, optimized, and emitted as EVM bytecode and ABI; compiler version affects output and gas behavior.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › Compilation Flow

Compilation: Solidity to Bytecode

Compilation Steps
1. Parse & Type-check
The compiler enforces types and ensures your code matches the pragma constraints.
2. Optimization
Optional optimizations reduce gas by reordering or collapsing operations.
3. Emit Bytecode & ABI
The bytecode is deployed, while the ABI describes how to call functions externally.
Concrete example
A setter that assigns a new value compiles down to a few storage write opcodes and stack operations. Different optimizer settings or compiler versions can change the exact opcodes and therefore influence gas cost. Inspecting the compilation artifact helps you reason about that cost.
Misconception
Assuming the same high-level code always compiles to identical bytecode. In reality, compiler version and optimization flags matter for both correctness and gas use.
Key Takeaway

Compile with a matching pragma, inspect warnings, and review ABI and bytecode to anticipate cost and behavior.

screens.title: Gas: The EVM's Fuel
screens.narratorSegment: Gas is the unit used to measure computational effort in the EVM. Each opcode and storage write has a gas cost, and the total gas consumed by a transaction determines how much the caller pays in Ether. Gas serves two primary purposes: it compensates miners or validators for processing work, and it prevents abusive or infinite computation by requiring callers to set a finite gas limit. A concrete scenario: when you deploy or call a state-changing function, you set a gas limit; if execution needs more gas than that, the EVM halts and reverts state changes while still consuming the gas used up to the halt. A common beginner mistake is underestimating gas for state-heavy operations or forgetting that view functions called from other contracts do consume gas when executed as part of a transaction. Another nuance is gas price versus gas limit: gas price determines how much Ether is paid per gas unit, and market conditions influence that price. Practical habits include measuring gas for common operations in test deployments and designing functions to minimize expensive storage writes. Before we move on, reflect on which operations in your contract could be costly and how you might refactor them to save gas.

keyIdea.text: Gas quantifies work; it must be paid in Ether and enforces limits to keep the network secure and efficient.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › Gas: The EVM's Fuel

Gas: The EVM's Fuel

Gas measures computational steps, limits execution, and determines transaction cost in Ether.

How gas works
  • Each EVM opcode has a fixed gas cost; storage writes are among the most costly operations.
  • Callers set a gas limit to bound execution; if the limit is exceeded, execution reverts.
  • Gas price sets the Ether-per-gas unit and is determined by network demand.
Concrete example
Calling a function that updates a state variable consumes gas for reading inputs, computing, and writing to storage. If you hit the gas limit, the EVM reverts state changes but consumes the paid gas.
Common mistakes & tips
  • Underestimating gas for loops or storage-heavy patterns can lead to reverts and lost fees.
  • Assume view functions cost no gas only when called off-chain by a read provider; in-contract calls may cost gas.
  • Measure and profile expensive paths in a testnet before mainnet deployment.
Key Takeaway

Treat gas as both a fee and a safety budget; design contracts to minimize expensive operations.

screens.title: Pragma and Compiler Versioning
screens.narratorSegment: The pragma directive declares which compiler versions your Solidity file is intended for and prevents accidental compilation with incompatible compiler releases. For example, a statement that indicates compatibility with 0.8. x ensures you don't compile with a version that introduces breaking changes. Compiler behavior changes over time — optimizations, safety checks, and even semantics can shift between releases — so a mismatched compiler may produce different bytecode or reveal new warnings. A concrete example: using a caret range like allows compiling with patch and minor updates in that range but avoids major version jumps. A typical beginner mistake is omitting pragma entirely or compiling with the wrong version in Remix, which often leads to confusing errors or subtle runtime differences. A practical habit is to set an explicit pragma that reflects the version you tested against and to lock build systems to that compiler during deployment. Another useful practice is to read compiler warnings and prefer stable releases for production builds. To close, think of pragma as a contract with your toolchain: it makes compilation predictable and helps you reason about how your source maps to the bytecode that will run on the EVM.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › Pragma & Compiler

Pragma and Compiler Versioning

What pragma does
It specifies a compiler version range so your code is compiled with a compatible compiler, reducing surprises from breaking changes or different optimizations.
Practical guidance
  • Include a pragma line such as to pin a compatible 0.8.x compiler range.
  • Match your build and deployment toolchain to the pragma to avoid runtime mismatches.
  • Resolve warnings before deployment and prefer tested compiler releases for production.
Misconception

Omitting pragma or using the wrong compiler is a common source of compile errors and subtle behavior changes; treat pragma as part of your contract’s specification.

screens.title: SimpleStorage: Structure and Meaning
screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk through a small storage contract to see how Solidity pieces map to on-chain behavior. The contract begins with a license and a pragma directive locking the compiler range. Next is the contract declaration, which groups state variables and functions. A state variable such as is stored permanently on-chain in a storage slot; marking it public creates an automatically generated getter. The setNumber function takes an input and assigns it to the state variable — that assignment is a storage write and therefore consumes gas when executed in a transaction. The getNumber function is declared view and returns the stored value; when called as a read-only off-chain call, it does not consume gas for the caller. A typical beginner misconception is to treat view functions as free in every context: if another contract calls a view function inside a transaction, that execution costs gas because it runs as part of the transaction. As a final point, remember immutability: once deployed, this contract’s code cannot be changed in place. A good learner question is: which lines of this contract will increase gas usage when executed and why?

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › SimpleStorage Walkthrough

SimpleStorage: Structure and Meaning

Key elements
  • Pragma directive pins the compiler range for reproducible builds.
  • Contract declaration groups state and behavior into a deployable unit.
  • State variables are persisted on-chain in storage slots.
  • Functions modify or read state; view functions indicate no state modification.
Example snippet
// SPDX-License-Identifier: MIT
pragma solidity ^0.8.0;

contract SimpleStorage {
  uint256 public myNumber;

  function setNumber(uint256 _newNumber) public {
    myNumber = _newNumber;
  }

  function getNumber() public view returns (uint256) {
    return myNumber;
  }
}
Explanation & checks
The setNumber function performs a storage write and therefore consumes gas when called in a transaction. The getNumber function is view and can be called without gas when used by off-chain readers. If another contract calls getNumber during its own transaction, the call costs gas because it runs inside that transaction.
Misconception

View functions are free only for external read calls. In-contract or transactional calls still consume gas.

screens.title: Counter Contract — Hands-on Activity
screens.narratorSegment: This hands-on walkthrough uses a counter contract to tie together concepts: state, constructor initialization, state-changing functions, and safety checks. The Counter contract declares a public count state variable initialized to zero in the constructor. The increment function performs a simple storage write to increase the counter, which costs gas when executed as a transaction. The decrement function includes a guard to avoid underflow by checking that the count is greater than zero before decrementing; this pattern illustrates exercising safe checks in contract logic. In practice you will paste the provided Counter code into a browser IDE and compile it with the pragma-specified compiler. Deploy it to a test network or the local JavaScript environment, then call increment and observe the gas used for that transaction. A common beginner mistake is to expect underflow to be silently allowed; modern compiler and language versions prevent unsafe underflow behaviors, but logic checks are still important for clarity. After you run the activity, check that the count increments and that decrement does nothing when the count is zero. Finally, reflect on how gas consumption increased when a transaction wrote state and what that implies for frequently called functions in larger contracts.

A common beginner mistake is to expect underflow to be silently allowed; modern compiler and language versions prevent unsafe underflow behaviors, but logic checks are still important for clarity. After you run the activity, check that the count increments and that decrement does nothing when the count is zero. Finally, reflect on how gas consumption increased when a transaction wrote state and what that implies for frequently called functions in larger contracts.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › Counter Activity

Counter Contract — Hands-on

Starter code
// SPDX-License-Identifier: MIT
pragma solidity ^0.8.0;

contract Counter {
    uint256 public count; // State variable to store the counter value

    constructor() {
        count = 0; // Initialize count to 0 when the contract is deployed
    }

    function increment() public {
        count = count + 1; // Increment the counter
    }

    function decrement() public {
        if (count > 0) {
            count = count - 1; // Decrement the counter
        }
    }

    function getCount() public view returns (uint256) {
        return count; // Return the current count
    }
}
Activity steps & checks
  1. Create Counter.sol in Remix and paste the code.
  2. Select a compiler matching the pragma, compile until no warnings remain.
  3. Deploy to a test environment and call increment; observe gas used on the transaction receipt.
  4. Call decrement at zero to confirm the guard prevents underflow.
Key Takeaway

Testing contracts in a safe environment helps you observe gas costs for storage writes and verify basic correctness before deployment.

screens.title: State Variables vs. Local Variables
screens.narratorSegment: Distinguishing state variables from local variables is essential for understanding costs and persistence. A state variable is stored permanently on-chain in storage slots and persists across transactions. Writing to state requires storage opcodes and therefore consumes gas. A local variable, by contrast, lives only during execution, usually in memory or on the stack; using it does not change persistent storage and is generally cheaper. For example, computing a temporary sum in a function using local variables avoids additional storage writes, reducing cost. A common misconception is that local variables are free — they still consume some gas for computation, but not the heavier cost of persistent storage writes. When designing functions, prefer local computation and minimize writes to state when possible. If you do need to update state, batch updates or emit events to reduce repeated costly operations. To test this, measure transaction receipts: calling a function that only computes a value and returns it often consumes far less gas than one that writes that value to a state variable. Consider which values truly need to persist across transactions and which can be computed transiently for better gas efficiency.

Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › State vs Local Variables

State Variables vs. Local Variables

Quick comparison
State Variable
Persists on-chain, stored in storage slots, expensive to write.
Local Variable
Ephemeral during execution, kept in memory or stack, cheaper to use.
Example
Compute a sum in local variables and return it instead of writing it to a state variable when persistence is not needed.
Design tips
  • Avoid unnecessary state writes in frequently called functions.
  • Batch updates to reduce multiple costly storage operations.
  • Use events to publish data off-chain when persistent on-chain state is not required.
Misconception

Local variables do cost some gas; they are not free but are far cheaper than persistent storage writes.

screens.title: Visibility and Function Modifiers
screens.narratorSegment: Function visibility and modifiers tell the compiler and runtime who can call a function and whether it modifies state. Visibility keywords such as public make functions callable externally, while internal or private restrict access. The view keyword signals that a function does not modify state, which allows off-chain callers to query state without paying gas. A concrete example is a public view getter for a state variable: calling it from an off-chain provider returns state without a transaction cost. However, a misconception to watch is thinking that marking a function view prevents gas cost in all contexts; if another contract calls that view function within a transaction, the call consumes gas as part of that transaction. Access control is another critical area: if you expect only certain accounts to run a function, you must include explicit checks or modifiers that enforce that rule. Neglecting proper visibility or access controls can lead to unintended public access and vulnerabilities. As you write functions, explicitly choose the narrowest visibility and add clear modifiers or require checks to enforce intended actors. After this, reflect on one function you’ve written and ask whether its visibility or modifiers align with intended access and gas expectations.

keyIdea.text: Visibility and modifiers control who can call functions and whether those calls modify state and cost gas.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › Visibility & Modifiers

Visibility and Function Modifiers

Common keywords
  • public: callable externally and internally; for state variables it creates a getter.
  • view: promises not to modify state; off-chain reads can be gas-free.
  • private/internal: restrict access inside the contract or inheritance tree.
Example question
If a function is marked view but called by another contract inside a transaction, will it consume gas? Yes — it runs as part of the caller's transaction and consumes gas.
Access control tip
For functions that should be restricted, add explicit checks such as verifying the caller address or using well-defined modifiers. Do not rely solely on 'private' to secure sensitive logic that depends on external conditions.
Misconception

Visibility keywords change accessibility but do not substitute for explicit authorization checks when sensitive actions are involved.

screens.title: Immutability and Security Considerations
screens.narratorSegment: One of the defining properties of smart contracts is immutability: once deployed, the contract code cannot be replaced in place. This immutability gives users confidence that the logic they rely on will not secretly change, but it also means bugs or insecure patterns are extremely costly to fix. A concrete example: if a contract incorrectly exposes a state-changing function to the public, that mistake persists after deployment until a planned upgrade or migration occurs. Therefore, secure design practices are essential: validate inputs, use access checks, avoid storing secrets, and minimize complex on-chain logic where possible. A common misconception is to assume immutability can be retroactively fixed by simply updating code; instead, planners use upgrade patterns such as proxies when upgrades are required, but those come with their own complexity and trust considerations. Before deployment, thorough testing, auditing, and using small, well-reviewed building blocks reduces risk. Another practical habit is to deploy first on test networks and verify gas usage and behavior. To finish, ask yourself: what could go wrong if a function were callable by anyone, and how could you enforce proper access before deployment?

keyIdea.text: Deployed contracts are permanent; design and test carefully to avoid costly post-deployment mistakes.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › Immutability & Security

Immutability and Security Considerations

Why immutability matters
Immutable code provides trust that deployed logic will not change unexpectedly. However, it also means errors are permanent and may require complicated migration or upgrade strategies.
Security checklist
  • Run unit and integration tests and compile with the exact pragma version.
  • Avoid storing secrets in state variables — on-chain data is public.
  • Enforce access controls with explicit checks and clear modifiers.
Common mitigation patterns
Use small, simple contracts when possible and perform staged deployments. When upgrades are necessary, plan and document upgrade mechanisms carefully and prefer minimal privileged surfaces. Test migrations on testnets first.
Misconception

Immutability does not mean you can never change behavior, but changing typically requires migration or explicit upgrade patterns which must be planned and trusted.

screens.title: Transaction Lifecycle and Out-of-Gas Behavior
screens.narratorSegment: A transaction lifecycle begins with a user or contract creating a signed transaction specifying a gas limit and optionally a gas price. The network picks the transaction, and when a miner or validator executes it, the EVM runs the compiled bytecode step by step. Each opcode consumes gas; the EVM tracks the remaining gas budget as execution proceeds. If execution finishes successfully within the gas limit, state changes are committed and the gas used is paid to the miner or validator. If the transaction runs out of gas mid-execution, the EVM reverts all state changes so that the chain returns to its previous state; however, the gas consumed until the revert is still paid. This mechanism both compensates work and prevents infinite loops or runaway computation. A concrete example: calling a function that performs an unbounded loop without a sufficient gas limit will consume gas until the budget is exhausted and then revert, leaving the chain state unchanged but costing the caller Ether. A common beginner mistake is setting an overly low gas limit and losing funds when a transaction reverts. As a practical habit, simulate transactions in a test environment, set conservative gas limits for complex calls, and examine transaction receipts to learn how gas was consumed. What part of a transaction's lifecycle would you like to inspect further?

keyIdea.text: Transactions carry a gas budget; if execution completes within it, state commits; if not, execution reverts but gas is still consumed.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › Transaction Lifecycle

Transaction Lifecycle and Out-of-Gas Behavior

Lifecycle steps
  1. Create and sign a transaction with a gas limit.
  2. Network picks the transaction and a validator executes bytecode in the EVM.
  3. Gas is consumed per opcode; if execution finishes, state commits and gas is paid.
  4. If gas is exhausted, execution reverts state changes but consumed gas is not refunded.
Practical guidance
Always test transactions locally or on a testnet, especially for operations that might be heavy. Read the transaction receipt to see gas used and any revert reason. When in doubt, set a higher gas limit but monitor actual gas used to optimize later.
Misconception

A revert returns state to its prior state, but it does not refund the gas already consumed; that cost is real.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.narratorSegment: Let's consolidate the most important ideas. First, Solidity is the contract-oriented language you use to declare persistent state and executable behavior that compiles to EVM bytecode. Second, the EVM is a deterministic, sandboxed runtime that applies the same rules on every node and charges gas for each operation. Third, gas measures computational effort and acts as both a fee and a resource safeguard; running out of gas reverts state changes but still consumes the gas used. Remember that pragma pins compiler versions for stable compilation and that state writes are significantly more expensive than local computation. A useful practice is to compile with a matching pragma, deploy to a testnet, and measure gas consumption for state-changing functions. Finally, design with immutability and access control in mind: assume your deployed contract is visible and permanent. Which of these core concepts will guide your next contract draft?

fullNarratorScript:
Welcome. In this chapter we explore Solidity, the contract-oriented language used to write transparent, immutable logic on Ethereum-compatible blockchains, and the Ethereum Virtual Machine that executes compiled contracts. You will learn how high-level Solidity maps to EVM bytecode, why the pragma directive locks a compiler range, and how gas measures the computational cost of every operation. Understanding these ideas helps you design secure, efficient contracts that deploy and run predictably. For example, a simple storage contract shows how state variables are written to the blockchain and how view functions can be used to read state without gas under a read-only call. A critical contrast to keep in mind is immutability: deployed contracts cannot be edited, so bugs must be prevented ahead of time. Finally, gas is both a fee and a safety: it compensates validators and prevents runaway code. As you go through this lesson set, you will compile a small counter contract, observe gas implications, and practice spotting common mistakes. By the end, you should be able to describe Solidity’s role, explain the EVM’s execution model, and reason about gas and cost trade-offs when designing contracts. What part of building a contract feels most uncertain to you right now?

In this chapter you will build a working mental model of Solidity and the Ethereum Virtual Machine. First, you will explain Solidity’s role as the high-level, contract-oriented language for writing smart contracts and contrast it with general-purpose languages. Second, you will describe the EVM’s architecture and how compiled bytecode is executed deterministically on every node. Third, you will identify the structural building blocks of a Solidity file — the pragma directive, contracts, state variables, and functions — and you will understand how those parts map to deployed behavior. Finally, you will grasp the concept of gas: how it measures computational effort, how users set gas limits and pay gas in Ether, and why gas both budgets resources and defends the network. Each objective pairs a clear skill with a quick example, such as compiling a small storage contract or running the counter in a browser IDE. These skills matter because they let you reason about cost, security, and correctness before you deploy immutable code. By the end you'll have four verified competency steps that prepare you to write, compile, and analyze simple smart contracts safely. Which objective do you want to start with?

This second objectives screen focuses on practice and safety. You will compile example contracts using a compiler version that matches the pragma directive, and you will run read-only calls to view functions without spending gas via a read provider. You will also deploy a simple counter contract and exercise increment and decrement to see gas consumption on state changes. During practice, pay attention to safety guidance: treat deployed contracts as immutable, avoid storing secrets on-chain, and plan for gas cost when designing frequently called functions. A practical misstep to watch for is skipping the pragma or using an incompatible compiler; that often causes confusing compile errors. Another is underestimating gas: operations that update state consume gas, so loops or unbounded structures can be expensive. Each practice step includes a short verification milestone so you can confirm correct compilation and expected gas behavior. These exercises train you to think like an auditor: anticipate costs, limits, and attack vectors before publishing immutable logic. Which practice milestone will you perform first in Remix?

Solidity is a high-level, contract-oriented language specifically designed to declare the rules, storage, and callable behavior of smart contracts on Ethereum and compatible chains. It borrows familiar syntax patterns from languages like JavaScript and C++ while adding contract-focused keywords and constructs. Define contracts like classes: they bundle state variables, functions, events, and access modifiers into a single deployable unit. A clear definition helps: Solidity is statically typed, which means every variable has a declared type such as an unsigned integer of 256 bits, and the compiler checks types before producing bytecode. For a concrete example, declaring a public uint256 variable creates both storage on-chain and an automatically generated getter function; that getter can be used off-chain without paying gas when called as a read. A common misconception is that Solidity behaves exactly like general-purpose scripting languages — it does not. Contracts run in a distributed, deterministic environment where every state change is recorded and costs gas. Another important point is that code compiled with one compiler version may behave differently under another, so the pragma directive matters for reproducible compilation. As you learn Solidity, practice by reading small contracts and mapping each keyword to its runtime consequence. What part of Solidity’s types or contract model do you want to inspect next?

The Ethereum Virtual Machine, or EVM, is the runtime that executes compiled smart contract bytecode on every full node. It behaves like a sandboxed, stack-based virtual machine: contracts are compiled from Solidity into low-level instructions that the EVM understands, and every node runs the same instructions deterministically. This deterministic behavior is essential so that all nodes reach the same state after processing identical transactions. The EVM also isolates contract execution from the host environment, preventing arbitrary node-level access. A concrete example: when you call a function that updates a state variable, the compiled bytecode executes a sequence of stack operations and storage writes; those writes are recorded as state changes only if the transaction completes within the provided gas budget. A common misconception is that the EVM is a centralized server — it is not; it is a runtime implemented by many independent nodes that apply the same rules. Why does this matter in practice? Determinism allows you to reason about contract outcomes and design tests that replicate on-chain behavior. One practical takeaway is to keep bytecode size and complexity reasonable, because more complex operations mean more gas and larger attack surface. After studying the EVM’s role, consider how your high-level code translates to low-level steps and how that affects cost and security.

Compilation transforms Solidity source into deployable bytecode that the EVM executes. The process begins with parsing your source file and checking types and syntax against the declared pragma range. The compiler then performs optimization and emits EVM bytecode plus optional metadata. Practically, you compile a file, inspect compiler output for warnings, and produce an artifact that can be deployed. A concrete example: writing a setter function in Solidity compiles down to a sequence of storage write opcodes in bytecode. One common misconception is that compilation is lossless in terms of developer intent; while semantics remain, optimizations can combine or reorder operations to reduce gas. That is why matching the compiler version specified by pragma is crucial — different versions may optimize differently or change semantics. In the Remix IDE you choose a compiler version that satisfies the pragma and view compilation warnings. A useful practice is to read the compiled bytecode size and the ABI. The ABI tells external callers how to encode function calls; the bytecode is what the EVM runs. As a closing thought, compiling is where abstraction meets execution, so use compilation as a safety gate: ensure warnings are addressed and the pragma is aligned with your selected compiler.

Gas is the unit used to measure computational effort in the EVM. Each opcode and storage write has a gas cost, and the total gas consumed by a transaction determines how much the caller pays in Ether. Gas serves two primary purposes: it compensates miners or validators for processing work, and it prevents abusive or infinite computation by requiring callers to set a finite gas limit. A concrete scenario: when you deploy or call a state-changing function, you set a gas limit; if execution needs more gas than that, the EVM halts and reverts state changes while still consuming the gas used up to the halt. A common beginner mistake is underestimating gas for state-heavy operations or forgetting that view functions called from other contracts do consume gas when executed as part of a transaction. Another nuance is gas price versus gas limit: gas price determines how much Ether is paid per gas unit, and market conditions influence that price. Practical habits include measuring gas for common operations in test deployments and designing functions to minimize expensive storage writes. Before we move on, reflect on which operations in your contract could be costly and how you might refactor them to save gas.

The pragma directive declares which compiler versions your Solidity file is intended for and prevents accidental compilation with incompatible compiler releases. For example, a statement that indicates compatibility with 0.8. x ensures you don't compile with a version that introduces breaking changes. Compiler behavior changes over time — optimizations, safety checks, and even semantics can shift between releases — so a mismatched compiler may produce different bytecode or reveal new warnings. A concrete example: using a caret range like allows compiling with patch and minor updates in that range but avoids major version jumps. A typical beginner mistake is omitting pragma entirely or compiling with the wrong version in Remix, which often leads to confusing errors or subtle runtime differences. A practical habit is to set an explicit pragma that reflects the version you tested against and to lock build systems to that compiler during deployment. Another useful practice is to read compiler warnings and prefer stable releases for production builds. To close, think of pragma as a contract with your toolchain: it makes compilation predictable and helps you reason about how your source maps to the bytecode that will run on the EVM.

A transaction lifecycle begins with a user or contract creating a signed transaction specifying a gas limit and optionally a gas price. The network picks the transaction, and when a miner or validator executes it, the EVM runs the compiled bytecode step by step. Each opcode consumes gas; the EVM tracks the remaining gas budget as execution proceeds. If execution finishes successfully within the gas limit, state changes are committed and the gas used is paid to the miner or validator. If the transaction runs out of gas mid-execution, the EVM reverts all state changes so that the chain returns to its previous state; however, the gas consumed until the revert is still paid. This mechanism both compensates work and prevents infinite loops or runaway computation. A concrete example: calling a function that performs an unbounded loop without a sufficient gas limit will consume gas until the budget is exhausted and then revert, leaving the chain state unchanged but costing the caller Ether. A common beginner mistake is setting an overly low gas limit and losing funds when a transaction reverts. As a practical habit, simulate transactions in a test environment, set conservative gas limits for complex calls, and examine transaction receipts to learn how gas was consumed.
